_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 600 words, six questions in text order). Test 3 leans on reference and purpose: two questions ask what 'this' or 'it' refers to, one asks why the writer mentions a detail. Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page and by Full test 3.
title: The winter keeper
subtitle: Novelist Owen Brady spent a winter looking after an empty hostel on a small Scottish island. He explains why he is going back.

cards.text: The advert was three lines long and appeared in a newspaper I almost never buy. A hostel on the island of Carra needed someone to look after it from November to March, when it was closed to visitors. Accommodation was free; wages were not mentioned. I read it twice, then cut it out and left it on the kitchen table, where it stayed for a week while I listed all the reasons it was a ridiculous idea. I had a novel to finish and no experience of looking after anything larger than a cat. In the end, those turned out to be the reasons I went.
cards.question: What does the writer say about his reaction to the advert?
choices: He applied as soon as he had read it.
He was put off at first by the lack of pay.
The arguments against going became his reasons for going.
He hoped somebody would talk him out of it.
cards.highlight: In the end, those turned out to be the reasons I went.
cards.why: 'Those' are the novel and his lack of experience, which he first listed against the idea. He waited a week, so A is wrong; the missing wages are mentioned but never said to worry him.

cards.text: The island has eleven permanent residents, a shop that opens on Tuesdays and Fridays, and a ferry that, in winter, runs when the weather allows. That, I learned in my first week, is not often. My duties were simple: check that the pipes did not freeze, keep the generator running and air the rooms once a week. The residents were friendly but busy, and for days at a time I saw no one at all. I had expected to find this difficult. What I had not expected was how quickly it stopped feeling like silence and started feeling like space.
cards.question: What does 'this' refer to in 'I had expected to find this difficult'?
choices: spending long periods without seeing anyone
the irregular ferry service
his duties in the hostel
the residents' busy lives
cards.highlight: for days at a time I saw no one at all
cards.why: 'This' points back to the sentence just before: days when he 'saw no one at all', which later 'stopped feeling like silence'. The residents' being busy is the cause, not the thing he found difficult.

cards.text: The novel, meanwhile, refused to cooperate. I had imagined that without interruptions I would write all day, every day. Instead I wrote for an hour in the morning and spent the afternoons doing things I would once have called a waste of time: walking the shore, mending a fence for a neighbour, learning the names of birds. For a month I felt guilty about this. Then I reread what I had written and realised that the hour each morning was producing the best pages I had ever written. The afternoons, it seemed, were where the work was really being done.
cards.question: What does the writer suggest about his afternoons?
choices: They made him fall behind with his novel.
They were spent mainly helping his neighbours.
They made him feel guilty for the whole winter.
They contributed more to his writing than he had realised.
cards.highlight: The afternoons, it seemed, were where the work was really being done.
cards.why: The afternoons were 'where the work was really being done': the walking and the birds fed the best pages. He felt guilty only 'for a month', not all winter; mending one fence is not 'mainly' helping.

cards.text: Not everything went smoothly. In January a storm took the roof off the hostel's shed and cut the power for four days. I had a torch, a stove and a great deal of tinned soup, so I was never in any real danger, but I was very cold and, for the first time, very lonely. On the third evening Morag, who runs the shop, walked a mile through the rain with a flask of tea and a bag of candles. She stayed for ten minutes, talked mainly about her goats, and left. I have rarely been so grateful for a conversation about goats.
cards.question: Why does the writer mention the conversation about goats?
choices: to show how little he and Morag had in common
to emphasise how much any company meant to him at that moment
to suggest that Morag felt uncomfortable visiting him
to explain why Morag could only stay for a short time
cards.highlight: I have rarely been so grateful for a conversation about goats.
cards.why: He was 'for the first time, very lonely', so even ten minutes about goats made him 'so grateful'. The joke is that the subject did not matter; the company did.

cards.text: By February I had settled into a routine that I was almost reluctant to share with anyone. Friends phoned to ask whether I was going mad. I told them I was fine, which was true, but I found it hard to explain why. The closest I came was in a letter to my sister, in which I said that on the island nothing was urgent, but everything mattered. She wrote back that it sounded like the opposite of my life in London, and she was right.
cards.question: What does 'it' refer to in 'it sounded like the opposite of my life in London'?
choices: the way the writer described life on the island
the friends' worried phone calls
the writer's fear of going mad
the novel the writer was finishing
cards.highlight: nothing was urgent, but everything mattered
cards.why: His sister is answering his letter, so 'it' is what he wrote there: 'nothing was urgent, but everything mattered'. It was his friends, not he, who wondered whether he was going mad.

cards.text: The hostel reopened in April, and I caught the first ferry of the season back to the mainland. The novel was finished two months later. Reviewers have been kind about it, and several have commented on how calm it feels, which makes me smile, since it was written by a man who spent much of that winter worrying about frozen pipes. People often ask whether I would go back. I already have. Next November I will be on Carra again, and this time I have not listed any reasons why I shouldn't.
cards.question: How does the writer feel about returning to Carra?
choices: He is anxious that a second winter will be harder.
He is going back mainly to write another novel.
He has no doubts about his decision.
He is unsure whether he has made the right choice.
cards.highlight: this time I have not listed any reasons why I shouldn't
cards.why: The first paragraph returns: last time he listed reasons not to go; this time he has listed none. Nothing is said about a new novel or about a harder winter.
